speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: asked the Minister for National Development in respect of paths on the Park Connector Network where one side of the path is marked "PCN" and the adjacent side has a sign of a person walking (a) whether cyclists or PMD riders are required to keep to the part marked "PCN"; (b) whether those who are on foot are required to keep to the side with the sign of a person walking; and (c) what are the measures taken to monitor and ensure safe usage of such paths by all users.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: So, less than 10% was taken in as part of this pilot.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: During the pilot period, NParks had carried out public outreach along these stretches.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For instance, NParks officers go onsite to educate PCN users on how to use the PCNs safely.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: NParks has also put up physical banners and standees to promote responsible track etiquette.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In addition, NParks has also been encouraging a "keep left" etiquette on our PCNs where slower users should keep left, while faster users overtake on the right.

speaker: The Second Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: NParks will also continue to work with LTA and the community to promote the safe and orderly use of our PCNs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have asked this question because I have observed that despite the markings, which I agree is quite helpful, actually, on the ground, a lot of people are not really following the markings.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It has caused certain confusion which I witnessed personally.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have also witnessed accidents where you have PMDs or bicycles on the part marked with the "foot", and then, on the PCN marking, you have people walking.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, may I ask if NParks can increase the public messaging on the safe use of these paths?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If we think of a PCN, typically, they are between 2.5 metres and four metres.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And it is a shared path – people who walk, brisk walk, jog, run, cycle, use mobility devices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is a shared space for people to move from place to place, for people to commute.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And so, for the PCN to be a safe space for everyone depends on a couple of factors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, clear markings make it easier for people to follow certain rules.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Or physically segregated pathways, so that you are very clear these are for pedestrians and these are for other users.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As the Member rightly pointed out, we need to continue this effort to share with all PCN users about the safe use of PCNs and the co-existence of different users of PCNs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Lastly, of course, and I think probably the most important, would be user consideration and etiquette and the behaviour and habits of all PCN users.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, a combination of all these will make the PCNs a much safer space for everyone.
